alerts.rationale: The configured OAuth2 endpoint is contacted synchronously with requests.post and no timeout, so a slow or nonresponsive endpoint can hold the login worker/request indefinitely; the endpoint is configuration-controlled and no timeout is set at this call site (lines 36–41, 60–62).

SHA-1 is used only to compare serialized event details for equality, not as a security mechanism; a collision could at most make change detection miss a difference. The hashed dictionaries are assembled from event fields and compared at lines 229–250.

The file-backed sharing database deserializes its records with unrestricted pickle at line 131, and does the same during directory-wide listing (lines 201–208); pickle can execute attacker-controlled reducers before the version check. The records are written as pickles by this code, but no integrity/authenticity validation of files is performed before loading, so a party able to place or alter a database file can trigger code execution when sharing records are read.

The list operation unconditionally unpickles every regular file found in the configured sharing database directory (lines 199–208), and there is no validation before deserialization. A crafted file in that directory can execute pickle payload code when a sharing listing is triggered; normal writes being produced by this application does not make the on-disk files safe if an attacker can modify them.

The sharing database files are read directly with pickle.load in the flagged update path (and likewise in retrieval/list/delete), with no validation before deserialization; a crafted pickle can execute arbitrary code during loading. These are filesystem-backed application data files, and their origin/permissions are not shown to be restricted to trusted writers, so attacker-writable database content makes this exploitable.

The sharing record is loaded directly with `pickle.load` after only checking that a file exists; the version check occurs after deserialization, so a crafted pickle in the sharing database can execute code before that check. The database files are read in other paths as well, and these lines show records are created as files, but do not establish protection against an attacker able to alter the database.

The cache entry is created locally with `pickle.dump` from a `CacheContent` tuple derived from parsed item fields, while reads use a filename based on the resource href and verify a hash before accepting the contents. The request-controlled resource text is not itself treated as pickle data, and the code shown provides no route for a remote user to supply arbitrary pickle bytes; this is a trusted, application-generated cache.

The unpickled file is an application-managed history cache entry, not content supplied through an upload: each normal update writes only `[etag, history_etag]` with `pickle.dump` after validating href as a safe path component. A malicious cache file would require write access to the server's filesystem/cache directory, which is outside the attacker-controlled request data path shown here.

The configured storage hook is intentionally executed as a shell command (`shell=True`, lines 98–103), and the command is formatted with request-derived `path`, `to_path`, `request`, and `user` values at lines 80–91. Although those values are shell-quoted, the hook itself is administrator-configured; attacker influence over its command template is not established here, but its interpolated data can affect the executed shell command and warrants a potential vulnerability label.

The client-controlled sync token is restricted to a 64-character lowercase hexadecimal name before it is used in the cache path (lines 39–54), and the corresponding pickle is created internally from the collection state via `pickle.dump` (lines 91–100). No request-provided pickle bytes reach `pickle.load`; exploitation would require an attacker to alter the server’s cache file outside the shown request flow.
